1.pericope_label: They came to Thessalonica, and Paul reasoned with them out of the Scriptures
debates: Why nothing was attempted at Amphipolis and Apollonia: Barnes reports the argument from the emphatic article that there was probably no synagogue in either, Ellicott that there was no Jewish population to give an opening, and Robertson that we simply do not know and that Luke leaves many gaps; Henry and Calvin refer it to the guidance of the Spirit, Henry supposing that Paul nevertheless stayed long enough to preach there and Calvin that he tried and failed, which is why Luke passes it over

How long Paul stayed at Thessalonica: Robertson argues that the three sabbaths mark only the period of free access to the synagogue and that the epistles imply a far longer stay, Wesley notes only that the days between are not excluded, and Ellicott takes the three sabbaths at face value as a measure of the respect Paul commanded

Whether the earlier turning to the Gentiles was final: Chrysostom answers that Paul did not leave the Jews alone because of his longing affection for them, while Calvin restrains the harder sentence to the particular company who had wickedly rejected the gospel
outliers: Wesley's inference from the pronouns that Luke was left behind at Philippi, the narrative ceasing here to speak of Paul's company as we and not resuming that style until they are together again much later
Ellicott's calculation that the two cities mark the stages at which the travellers rested, thirty Roman miles a day being a toilsome rate for men so recently scourged

Calvin's excursus against those who deny that any certainty can be gathered out of the Scriptures, with the reproach that the word of God was more reverenced in an unbelieving nation, since the Jews at least admitted Paul and suffered him while he disputed from it
Chrysostom's account of the strategy, that they hastened past the small cities and pressed on to the greater, since from those the word was to flow as from a fountain into the neighbouring cities
Chrysostom's remark that the Passion is preached before all other things, so little were they ashamed of it, knowing it to be the cause of salvation
themes: the founding of the Thessalonian church

3.pericope_label: Opening and alleging that the Christ must needs have suffered
debates: Who the men of the market-place were: Clarke, following Hesychius and the Jewish use of the word for judges, takes them for a low kind of lawyers or pettifoggers deliberately employed because they carried juridical credit, and cites a Latin version that renders the phrase simply certain lawyers, while Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson all take them for the idlers and loungers of the agora, the standing material of a mob

The text of the fifth verse: Clarke judges the evidence strongest against both the clause about unbelief and the clause about envy and would omit them, Gill reports the first omitted by the Alexandrian copy, the Vulgate and the Syriac, Ellicott finds each wanting in different manuscripts, and Robertson nevertheless expounds the jealousy at length

Whether lewd is a bad rendering: Barnes calls it unhappy on the ground that the word is not in the original, while Ellicott defends it in its older sense of vile or worthless and traces it back further still to the plain meaning of an untaught layman
outliers: Wesley's answer to the freethinkers who observe that women are more religious than men and impute it to weakness of understanding, that in a religion which means taking up the cross women lie under a natural disadvantage of courage, so their embracing it was the stronger evidence of a power perfected in weakness
Clarke's explanation that the Jews, being too few to raise a mob themselves, cunningly employed men who had some standing about the courts, so that the charge of sedition would carry weight
Barnes's reflection that a mob regards very little the cause it is engaged in, and that the profane and the worthless often become violently enraged for the honour of religion

Ellicott's suggestion that Jason, though the name was locally conspicuous from the Argonaut and the tyrant of Pheræ, was most likely the Greek equivalent of Joshua, as it was for the apostate high priest of the Maccabean history
Calvin's three questions about Christ, whether he be, who he is, and what he is, with his observation that only the first two needed proving among Jews

6.pericope_label: They dragged Jason before the rulers of the city
debates: What the security taken of Jason was: Gill reads it as satisfaction given by the defence they made, and Clarke as enough for the present to prove the apostles upright, while Barnes reports the harder views that the pledge was to leave the city or that Jason would harbour them no more, and Ellicott and Robertson take it as a formal money bail, Robertson inferring that the condition was that Paul and Silas depart and not return

Which law of Caesar was appealed to: Ellicott takes it of the edict of Claudius, binding strictly only at Rome and in the colonies but showing the drift of imperial policy, while Robertson looks rather to the older statutes of treason

Whether the charge of proclaiming another king had any foothold: Clarke insists the apostles never insinuated that the kingdom was of this world and Calvin that the Jews knew a spiritual kingdom did the empire no injury and caught at the pretence maliciously, while Ellicott allows that the prominence of the coming of Christ as King in the Thessalonian preaching may itself have furnished the materials of the accusation
outliers: The politarch inscription: a title once cited as evidence of Luke's blundering, since found in seventeen inscriptions, five of them from Thessalonica, and now used as a proof of his accuracy; Ellicott describes the arch that carries it as still spanning a street of the modern city, Robertson as preserved in a museum

Ellicott's note that the same inscription carries names identical with those of converts in the apostolic history, and that there appear to have been seven magistrates bearing the title, as with the Archons of Athens
Clarke's aside that turning the world upside down was the very character his own forefathers bore for preaching the gospel in every part of the land
Barnes's report that the Roman people, and after them the emperors, would not permit the name of king to be used in a vanquished province except by their own permission
Calvin's refusal of the perverse wisdom of those who would purchase quiet by giving place to slander, since we must stand stoutly for the truth and be ready to hear evil for things done well

10.pericope_label: The Bereans searched the Scriptures daily, whether those things were so
debates: Whether the word rendered more noble means better born or better disposed: Calvin stands alone in referring it to nation and family rather than to the mind, answering the argument from the comparative form and observing that principal women had already believed at Thessalonica, while Gill, Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Wesley all take it of temper and conduct, the generous and teachable disposition ideally supposed to belong to noble birth

Why they withdrew by night: Barnes and Clarke read it as flight for safety once the foundation of a church was laid, while Henry insists the command to flee from city to city intends the flight for the carrying on of the work rather than for safety, and Calvin passes over the flight to marvel at the constancy that entered the next synagogue at once

Whether the readiness of the Bereans was native to them: Clarke reckons them a better educated and more polished people, Ellicott describes a temper predisposed to faith which yet would not take assertion for proof, and Gill enters the caveat that no man is naturally disposed to regard the gospel, there being a natural enmity in the mind against it
outliers: Ellicott's remark that the Berean converts have naturally been made a representative case by those who urge the duty, or claim the right, of private judgment, as occupying a middle position between credulity and scepticism to be reproduced in successive ages
Robertson's aside that in Scotland the people keep the Bible open before them while the preacher expounds the passage, a fine habit worth imitating
Henry's turn of phrase that out of the eater came forth meat and the devil was outshot in his own bow, the persecution intended to stop the gospel being overruled to further it
Clarke's citation of the Jewish maxim that none was of a noble spirit who did not employ himself in the study of the law

The disagreement of the modern notices: Ellicott gives the town twenty thousand inhabitants under a name still preserving the ancient one, Robertson some six thousand, and Barnes reports a surviving medal of Berea inscribed of the second Macedonia
themes: flight and the furtherance of the gospel

debates: Whether the withdrawal to the sea was a feint: Barnes denies that any sleight is implied, Clarke rejects the notion as unnecessary and assumes a voyage, and Ellicott reports the better manuscripts reading as far as the sea and argues from the absence of intermediate place-names that Paul sailed, while Robertson leaves the route open and reports the contrary conjecture that Paul gave the Jews the slip by travelling overland when they expected him to sail

Who the honourable Greek women were: Clarke takes them for mere heathens rather than proselytes, Ellicott for Gentile converts of the upper class as at Thessalonica, Wesley says the women were followed by their husbands, and Robertson infers instead that Luke implies the men also were Greeks of rank
How the twelfth verse connects with what precedes: Calvin denies that it picks out a few from those just named, which he calls absurd, and reads it of many more being added by their example
outliers: Barnes's excursus on the causes of unbelief, closing with the admission of Thomas Paine that he wrote the first part of the Age of Reason with neither Bible nor Testament to refer to, though he was writing against both, and could procure none where he then was

Calvin's insistence that behind the pursuit it is not men who procure the war but Satan, who uses his own as fans to raise sedition and will never cease to weary Christ's servants by open war, secret ambush, or domestic combat

Ellicott's observation that when the escort turned back Paul was, for the first time since the commencement of his missionary labours, absolutely alone, and that his yearning for company shows in the urgency of the message he sent
Robertson's remark that Silas and Timothy remaining behind would serve to screen the flight, since the Jews wanted Paul's blood and not theirs

Clarke's measurement of Athens at a hundred and seventy-eight stadia, or twenty-two Roman miles, in circumference in its most flourishing state, with the note that everything is now in a state of ruin

16.pericope_label: His spirit was stirred in him, for he saw the city full of idols
debates: What Paul made of the art of Athens: Ellicott holds that his sense of beauty in art was probably weak in any case and wholly overpowered by horror at the worship of what human hands had made, Barnes records only that no admiration is anywhere reported of a city that surpassed all others in the arts, Henry approves the indifference as proper in a man who had learned to call such learning a vain thing, and Robertson by contrast dwells at length on the Academy, the Lyceum, the Porch and the Garden and calls the city the art centre of the world

Whether Paul meant to preach at Athens at all: Wesley thinks he had no such design and that zeal drew him in unawares before his companions arrived, while Ellicott treats the disputing in the market-place as a deliberate new experiment undertaken after watching others dispute there, and Robertson holds simply that he could not remain still with the idolatry around him

Why Athens in particular: Calvin holds that the Lord suffered the mansion-house of wisdom to fall into extreme madness so that every age might learn what human wit can do in matters concerning God, while Chrysostom observes instead that Paul met greater trials among the Jews than among the Gentiles, the opposition here going no further than ridicule
outliers: The same joke of Petronius, that at Athens one might more easily meet with a god than with a man, quoted independently by Barnes, Clarke and Henry, the last two in the Latin; Barnes adds the testimonies of Pausanias, Lucian and Livy and Clarke gives the Pausanias in Greek
Henry's report that the city remained incurably addicted to idolatry long after the empire became Christian, and that all the pious edicts of the Christian emperors could not root it out
Gill's claim that Jews had long been settled at Athens and that this is how the Athenian philosophers came by their acquaintance with Jewish books, from which he holds they borrowed many things

Robertson's comparison of the casual hearers in the market-place with those who stop for street preaching or a harangue from a box in a public park, and his note that Paul may have stood near the Painted Porch where Zeno once taught
Calvin's corollary that religion is attributed to the devout alone, so that nothing remains for the rest but the reproach of atheism, however anxiously they torment themselves in superstition

18.pericope_label: Certain philosophers encountered him, and brought him unto the Areopagus
debates: Whether Paul was on trial at the Areopagus: Gill, Barnes, Wesley and Calvin all deny it, finding no accusation, no witnesses and none of the forms of trial, and taking the removal as a search for a better audience; Ellicott alone argues that the Court was probably sitting, since there would otherwise be no reason to take him there rather than to the Pnyx and since a member of the Court was among the converts, and settles on a preliminary inquiry without formal indictment; Robertson allows an examination as to the legality of the new teaching but holds the day for a criminal trial on such a charge had passed

Whether Epicurus taught what the Epicureans practised: Clarke doubts that the founder maintained the doctrines his school held, Barnes distinguishes the regulated pleasure he meant from the voluptuousness they embraced, Gill divides the sect into a strict and a loose sort, and Ellicott reports that the founder’s own life was marked by self-control and even piety and patriotism

Where Paul actually stood: Robertson doubts the familiar picture of the summit, there being no room there for a large gathering and the Court commonly meeting in a portico opening on the market-place, while Barnes describes the hill itself as an almost inaccessible mass of stone and Clarke and Ellicott describe the tribunal rather than the site
outliers: Clarke's etymology of the word rendered babbler, literally a collector of seeds and the name of a small bird that lives by picking them up on the road, transferred to men who gathered the sayings of others without order or method

Wesley's defence of the Athenians' mistake in taking Jesus and the Resurrection for a god and a goddess, since they might as well count the resurrection a deity as shame and famine and many others, together with his aside that Athens was a seminary of philosophers, who have ever been the pest of true religion

Clarke's description of the court sitting uncovered and by night, so that nothing should distract the judges and the sight of the accused should move them to neither pity nor aversion, with pleaders forbidden to work upon the passions and the parties sworn between the bleeding members of the victims
Calvin's citation of Horace, that one should fly a demander of questions since the same is also a blab, with his comparison of curious men to leaking barrels

The disagreement over the court's composition: Wesley gives its original number as twelve, afterwards increased to three hundred, while Ellicott says it consisted at first only of those who had filled the office of Archon and were over sixty

20.pericope_label: Ye men of Athens, I perceive that in all things ye are very religious
debates: What the word rendered too superstitious means: Barnes calls the rendering most unhappy, the term properly denoting reverence toward the gods and being used in a good sense by the classic writers, Clarke turns it into an acknowledgment that they are greatly addicted to religious practices and the ground of an appeal for a fair hearing, and Robertson reports a neutral word used either way, thinks it unlikely Paul would open with an insult, and notes that how one takes it colours the whole speech; Calvin holds instead that superstition is exactly the charge, the word denoting the immoderate fear with which superstitious men torment themselves

How the discourse is to be framed: Calvin divides it into five members ending with Christ and the resurrection, and holds the four preceding heads had to be handled before the gospel could be reached, while Henry frames it by contrast with the sermons to Jews, where the business was to open and allege that Jesus is the Christ, and Wesley finds its shape in the audience’s own appetite for news, Paul beginning with first things and going on to last things

Whether the removal to the court had a legal ground: Clarke says he was called before the Areopagus on the authority of the laws forbidding the introduction of new deities, Robertson insists he does not speak as a man on trial at all, and Ellicott allows that if the Court was sitting the temptation to have recourse to it, if only to cause a sensation and terrify the stranger, may have been irresistible
outliers: Clarke's application of the Athenian itch for news to the London of his own day, where even ministers of the gospel have become Athenians in this sense, the book of God being neither read nor studied with half the avidity given to a newspaper

The same ancient witnesses to Athenian curiosity assembled independently by Barnes and Clarke, with Ellicott adding the description of the society prattler who asks whether there is anything new and then whether there is anything newer still

Ellicott's staging of the scene, the Court sitting in the open air on benches forming three sides of a quadrangle at the head of a flight of sixteen steps cut in the rock, with the temple of the Eumenides below, the Theseum to the east, and the Parthenon and the colossal bronze Athena facing him
Calvin's fourth head, that nothing is more absurd than to figure God by statue or picture, seeing that the mind of man is his true image
Wesley's exclamation at the encounter, Paul against Athens

23.pericope_label: To the unknown God: him declare I unto you
debates: Whether Paul altered the inscription: Clarke passes on the ancient charge that he found it in the plural and quoted it in the singular so as not to seem to acknowledge many gods, and calls it a most foolish saying since such a begging of the question would have wrecked his defence, while Calvin rejects the charge on the different ground that the inscription was in every man’s mouth and left no room for craft, and Robertson notes independently that an ancient traveller does speak of altars at Athens to gods unknown in the plural

Who raised the altar and to whom: Wesley reports the supposition that Socrates set it up to express covertly his devotion to the one true God, and the other that it honoured the God of Israel, whose name was never made known to the Gentiles, a view Clarke also reports, while Robertson gives a wholly different account, that in a pestilence a sheep was to be offered to the befitting god whoever he might be, since an altar dedicated to the wrong deity would provoke the anger of the rest

Whether the Athenians can be said to have worshipped God at all: Calvin raises the difficulty himself, that God refuses every worship not agreeable to his word and that Christ condemned the Samaritans for worshipping what they knew not, and answers it by the principle that God cannot be rightly worshipped until he is first made known
outliers: Robertson's report of the stern verdict that the inscription was the confession at once of a bastard philosophy and a bastard religion, against which he sets the apostle's readiness to seize on it as evidence of a deeper religious sense, and his note that our word agnostic descends from the adjective

Ellicott's observation that the words about temples made with hands reproduce what the persecutor had heard from Stephen, the very claim that once drove him to fanaticism, now extended to every temple raised by hands, with his corollary that Christian churches are holy not because God dwells in them but because they are set apart
Clarke's report from Oecumenius that the altar's full inscription ran, to the gods of Asia and Europe and Africa, to the unknown and strange God
The same two ancient quotations about swearing by the unknown God at Athens are produced by both Barnes and Clarke, but under different authors' names
Calvin's note that with profane men the proofs had to be drawn from nature itself, since it would have been in vain to contend with them by citing testimonies of Scripture
themes: the altar to the unknown God

25.pericope_label: He hath made of one blood all nations, that they should seek the Lord
debates: Whether the word blood belongs to the text: Clarke reports it omitted by leading manuscripts, several versions and early writers, and Robertson calls it a later explanatory addition, while Gill retains it and notes only that the Vulgate reads of one and the Arabic of one man

How far the groping could succeed: Barnes holds it was possible to find God from his works though with difficulty, which leaves idolatry without excuse, Calvin that God has engraven such manifest marks that even blind men may find them by groping, so that men are not merely blind but blockish, Wesley that feeling stands midway between seeking and finding and that God lays no force upon man, and Ellicott that the doubting particle implies the end was never reached in its completeness, the altar to the Unknown being the witness of the failure

Whether the rebuke of ceremonies touches the Mosaic worship as well: Calvin raises the objection himself and answers that the faithful never placed the worship of God in ceremonies but counted them helps to their infirmity, whereas the Gentiles reckoned that images, incense and shows discharged the offices of godliness
outliers: Clarke's report of the Athenian conceit that they were self-produced aboriginals, with the ancient gibe that the first men sprang up in Attica like radishes; Robertson notes the same claim to be indigenous and a special creation

Barnes's conclusion from the common descent of all men that no part of the race has any right to enslave or oppress another on account of a difference of complexion, supported with verses from a poet of his own century

Ellicott's concession that the apostle naturally took the account of creation as it came to him, but that the truth of the unity of mankind would remain even if other theories of the origin of species and the history of man were accepted
Robertson's report that Helen Keller, when told of God, said that she knew of him already, groping in the dark after him
Clarke's gloss that the continued power to respire and to extract from the atmosphere what supports animal life is as much the continued gift of God as life itself

28.pericope_label: In him we live and move; now God commandeth all men everywhere to repent
debates: What the overlooking of the times of ignorance means: Gill takes it as contempt and indignation, God leaving them without revelation or prophets in evidence of his displeasure, Ellicott and Barnes as forbearance, ignorance mitigating the guilt and so the punishment of the heathen world, and Robertson as merely negative, God having objected to polytheism all along, with both Ellicott and Robertson rejecting the suggestion of condoning that the received rendering carries

Whether the three verbs ascend or descend: Robertson reads them as an ascending scale climaxing in existence, while Calvin ranks life the most excellent, motion next and bare being least, and holds the apostle put the highest first; Ellicott parses them instead as the animal life, the emotional nature, and the essential being of intellect and will

Who the poet quoted was: Wesley makes him an Athenian of nearly three hundred years before, Robertson names him a man of Cilicia, and Clarke says expressly that your own poets means Grecian poets rather than men born at Athens, noting that a hymn of another philosopher has the same words with a single letter altered
outliers: Ellicott's judgment that the apostle's tone toward idolatry differs from the burning scorn and derision of the older prophets, as of one who has studied the genesis of idolatry and can speak of it, though not with tolerance, yet with pity for its victims
Wesley's stroke against Stoic necessity, that the universal demand of repentance bore down the idle plea of fatality, since no one could repent of doing what he could not but have done

Calvin's refusal to say why God suffered men to walk in darkness four thousand years, holding that where Scripture conceals the reason sobriety is worth more than preposterous wisdom, together with his observation that the appeal to what has been received from the beginning is the buckler behind which every abomination fortifies itself
Robertson's note that the apostle knew the line was written of Zeus and not of the God of Israel, and applied only the idea in it, with his report of allusions elsewhere to other Greek writers

Wesley's paraphrase that the beams of God's eye did in a manner shoot over the times of ignorance, and his description of the hymn quoted as one of the purest pieces of natural religion in all pagan antiquity
themes: in him we live and move

31.pericope_label: Some mocked, and others said, We will hear thee again of this matter
debates: Whether Athens was a failure: Henry says few were the better and the gospel had as little success there as anywhere, Calvin infers from the naming of a single man and a single woman that few believed at first, and Ellicott points the contrast with the great multitude at Thessalonica and Berea, while Robertson answers that no sermon is a failure which brings a company of men to believe and that a group was left strong enough to keep the fire burning, and Barnes holds the conversion of one man worth the labour

Why the discourse ended where it did: Clarke holds Paul had not finished and was about to preach salvation through Christ crucified, and Barnes that the derision caused a disturbance, both comparing the interruption of Stephen; Wesley blames the indolence of some hearers and the petulancy of others; Ellicott hears indignation in the apostle himself, declining to expose his Lord’s name to the jests of scoffers; Chrysostom asks instead why he was in such haste to leave a city where no danger threatened, and answers that he knew he would do them no great good

What is to be made of the writings under the convert’s name: Clarke reports the conjectures that he was first bishop of Athens and a martyr and that the woman was his wife, citing a judgment that all this has little foundation, Ellicott dates the treatise on the heavenly hierarchy centuries later, Wesley calls the writings spurious and fathered on him by men fond of high-sounding nonsense, and Calvin says it is too gross to ascribe them to him, while Robertson repeats the tradition of the bishopric and martyrdom without comment
outliers: Ellicott's account of how the day of judgment would have sounded to that audience, as a relapse into a popular mythology which their own satirists said not even boys believed any longer, with the Stoic maxim that the world's story is itself its judgment day

Henry's report of the maxim of their schools, that from privation to possession there is no return and life once lost is irrecoverable, with his note that they had deified their heroes after death but never thought of their being raised
Robertson's question, after the apostle walked out of Athens never to return, whether he had failed

Chrysostom's explanation of Athenian inattention, that hearing strange things was not really their study but only always having something to say, and his judgment that it seemed to Paul sufficient to have cast the seeds of the doctrines
Ellicott's report that legend has since transformed the convert into the patron saint of France, and that a church dedicated to him stands on the Areopagus of the modern city
